cols.text: Paper 1 - HL and SL same exam

items.html: This paper is the same for SL and HL students.
Three months prior to the examination the IB will release a statement with two elements.

The first element will be a small number of topics that provide context to the case study. These topics will not be topics that are in the guide but ones that students are asked to research for approximately five hours.
The second element will be the first 200 words, approximately, of the case study itself.
Overall, the case study will have 800 - 1000 words. The questions will be mainly qualitative, however some minor calculations might be required.

Most questions will be quantitative, though some questions may not have a quantitative element.
Students will receive an examination booklet with questions based on the stimulus material seen for the first time during the examination.
This paper is HL only
It will be about a social enterprise and requires students to identify and describe a human need and the potential organizational challenges facing the social entrepreneur wanting to meet this need.
Further to this, students are required to write a decision-making document that includes a business recommendation.

cols.html: Porter argued that every successful business must have a competitive advantage to prevent profits being eroded by rival businesses entering the market.
cols.text: Porter argued that every successful business must have a competitive advantage to prevent profits being eroded by rival businesses entering the market.

cols.html: A Competitive advantage refers to any factor that enables a business to be more differentiated and appealing to customers, such as having a unique selling point, or being able to produce goods or services better or cheaply than its rivals.
cols.text: A Competitive advantage refers to any factor that enables a business to be more differentiated and appealing to customers, such as having a unique selling point, or being able to produce goods or services better or cheaply than its rivals.

cols.html: Porter suggested that there are three generic or broad strategies that any business can use to sustain a competitive advantage:
cols.text: Porter suggested that there are three generic or broad strategies that any business can use to sustain a competitive advantage:

cols.html: Cost leadership is a generic strategy that aims to establish a competitive advantage by achieving the lowest operational costs in the market for a particular good or service. It means to become the lowest cost supplier of a product within the market.
cols.text: Cost leadership is a generic strategy that aims to establish a competitive advantage by achieving the lowest operational costs in the market for a particular good or service. It means to become the lowest cost supplier of a product within the market.

cols.html: Examples include providers of low-cost accommodation (such as youth hostels) and budget airlines - Ryan Air, Air Asia
cols.text: Examples include providers of low-cost accommodation (such as youth hostels) and budget airlines - Ryan Air, Air Asia

items.html: Economies of scale - Operating on a larger scale can enable firms to gain from lower unit costs of production. These cost-saving benefits of being large enable the business to charge lower prices whilst maintaining their profit margins.

Improved supply chains - Having more efficient methods of distribution also help to reduce costs of production. Some businesses own their suppliers, thereby avoiding the profit margins in the form of higher prices otherwise charged by their suppliers. Some supermarket chains, for example, own their own farms that supply their products. Zara, the Spanish clothes retail giant, also owns many of its suppliers. IKEA, the world's largest furniture retailer, designs and develops all its own products.
Relocation - A business can be located nearer to its suppliers and/customers in order to reduce transportation and distribution costs.

Insourcing production - Firms may be able to manufacture goods and/or provide services in-house at a lower cost than an outsourced third-party provider. This may be due to efficiency gains by insourcing and/or due to the profit margin imposed by outsourced providers.

cols.html: Remember that cost leadership, as a generic strategy, is about minimizing the cost to the business that is supplying goods or services. This is not the same as the price of the product that is charged to customers.

cols.html: It is not always clear which of Porter's generic strategies is used by a particular business, if used at all. In reality, firms sometimes use hybrid strategies, which combine elements of Porter’s generic strategies, in order to create competitive advantages. For example, large supermarkets chains (like Aldi, Lidl, Target, and Walmart) combine their low cost strategy with offering unique products or services. This helps them to attract more customers with competitive prices and unique product offerings.

cols.html: Hence, Essentially - Characteristics of a strong RQ:
cols.text: Hence, Essentially - Characteristics of a strong RQ:

items.html: Focused and specific

sub: It should target one clear decision or issue faced by the business.
Avoid being too broad (e.g., “How can Starbucks improve profitability?” is too vague).
Instead: “Should Starbucks introduce plant-based milk alternatives in Mexico City stores to increase revenue?”

items.html: Decision-oriented

sub: The RQ should help a manager/owner make a decision.
Good phrasing: “Should…”, “To what extent should…”, “Which option would be more effective…”.

items.html: Linked to the syllabus

sub: Must allow you to apply BM concepts, tools, and theories (SWOT, Ansoff, decision trees, ratios, etc.).
Examiners want to see that your analysis is rooted in IB BM theory, not just description.

items.html: Feasible with primary + secondary data

sub: You need to gather information (interviews, surveys, observations, financial data, etc.).
If you can’t realistically collect the evidence, it won’t work.

items.html: Context-specific

sub: Tie it to a real business with a real issue.

items.html: “How can Coca-Cola improve marketing?” (too broad, no clear decision)
“What is the best strategy for Tesla in the future?” (too speculative, vague)
“Should a local bakery in Monterrey introduce online delivery to increase sales revenue?”
“To what extent should Gym X raise its membership fees to improve profitability?”
“Which market entry method should Brand Y use to expand into Guatemala — franchising or joint venture?”

cols.html: A quick test: A good RQ will make you think: If I were the manager, would this question help me decide what to do next?
cols.text: A quick test: A good RQ will make you think: If I were the manager, would this question help me decide what to do next?

cols.html: 2 markers - Generally speaking, for definitions, you want to keep this concise to two sentences. I recommend for the first sentence to highlight the key aspects/features of the BM terminology. Your second sentence can highlight the aim/purpose/intention of the said BM term. For example, if you are asked to define the term predatory pricing, your first sentence can highlight what predatory pricing is about. Second sentence can be something like "It aims to drive the competitors out of the market completely, but is often an illegal method". Giving a quick and small example wherever possible is also recommended.

cols.html: 4 markers - these are usually phrased using the "Explain" command term. So you probably want to structure this using the PEE+L structure for each of the "two" things you're asked in the question (e.g. explain one advantage and one disadvantage of .....). For your reference, P (point - e.g. the advantage point, which is often found in the textbook/notes), E (explain the point - usually the theory of what that point means), E (evidence/example - this means you need to explain the advantage or disadvantage point in relation to the case study), and I (impact to business - this is where you want to talk about how the advantage or disadvantage point has an impact to the business and/or its stakeholders).
